wikipedia.title: Flitter Dance
categories: Performing arts in the Isle of Man

profile.name: Flitter Dance
profile.tagline: A traditional Manx processional dance performed on Good Friday.
profile.insight: The Flitter Dance features a distinctive stamping step, which folklorist Mona Douglas suggested was used to extinguish the live embers of fires built on the beach for cooking flitters.
profile.profile: The Flitter Dance (Flitter Daunsey) is a traditional folk dance from the Isle of Man, historically linked to Good Friday coastal rituals. It follows a processional structure and is characterized by a unique stamping step and the Manx Balance. Today, the dance is maintained as a living tradition, popular among younger dancers and community groups.
profile.profile_long:
The Flitter Dance, known in the Manx language as Flitter Daunsey, is a traditional dance originating from the Isle of Man. Its history is inextricably linked to the Good Friday custom of gathering and eating 'flitters' (limpets) on the shore. Historically, these shellfish were cooked in fires built on the beach using 'mychurachan' (seaweed) and accompanied by 'arran-traaie' (barley meal cakes). The remnants of this meal were cast into the sea with a prayer or charm, 'Gow shoh as bannee orrin' ('Take this and bless us'), marking the transition to the dance itself. Folklore suggests this ceremony is a survival of an ancient Gaelic ritual of propitiation or sacrifice to the powers of the sea.

The collection of the dance was a multi-decade effort by Mona Douglas. In 1937, she noted the dance as 'partly noted but still incomplete,' having received accounts of its existence from Mrs. Callow of Cardle Veg. It was not until 1957 that Douglas finalized the collection, gathering the specific steps from Mrs. Teare of Ballaugh, Ada Skillicorn, and Mrs. Radcliffe of Maughold. These informants provided the technical details that had been missing for years, including the distinctive stamping step. Douglas hypothesized that this stamping was intended to extinguish the embers of the beach fires used during the preceding meal.

While early accounts suggested the dancers moved in an S-shape, the version published in 'Rinkaghyn Vannin' in 1983 describes the dance in a 'processional form,' which remains the standard for modern performances. The dance is structured in two distinct halves: the first consists of the stamping steps, and the second comprises two sets of side-steps followed by the 'Manx Balance,' a signature movement involving a swinging, kicking motion of the foot. After these sequences, dancers rejoin their partners and repeat the pattern.

The dance was brought back into the public sphere in the 1960s by the Manx Folk Dance Society. Under the supervision of Mona Douglas, the first modern performance took place on 18 April 1960 at Ballakermeen School for members of the English Folk Dance and Song Society. Today, the dance is considered a living tradition, favored for its simple and repetitive structure, making it highly accessible for beginners and young dancers. The accompanying air, also collected by Douglas, is regarded as one of the oldest traditional Manx tunes.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated as part of a Good Friday coastal ritual on the Isle of Man involving the consumption of flitters. It was collected by Mona Douglas between 1937 and 1957. The Manx Folk Dance Society revived the dance in 1960.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in a processional form. It consists of two halves: a sequence of stamping steps, followed by two sets of side-steps and the 'Manx Balance,' which is a swinging, kicking motion of the foot.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is a traditional Manx air, which Mona Douglas described as potentially the oldest of all Manx tunes. It is played to accompany the processional movement.
sections.costume_and_setting: Historically performed on the beach following a meal of flitters and barley cakes. Modern performances take place in community settings and schools.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Traditionally associated with Good Friday, the dance is linked to an ancient Gaelic ceremony of propitiation or sacrifice to the sea.
sections.notable_figures: Mona Douglas (collector), Mrs. Callow, Mrs. Teare, Ada Skillicorn, and Mrs. Radcliffe (informants).
sections.lineage: A survival of an ancient Gaelic ceremony of propitiation or sacrifice to the powers of the sea.

profile.sacred_note: The dance and its associated food-throwing ritual are described as a survival of an ancient Gaelic ceremony of propitiation or sacrifice to the powers of the sea.

teaching.level_notes: Simple and repetitive form, suitable for beginners and young dancers.

movement_profile.footwork: Stamping steps, side-steps, and the Manx Balance (swinging/kicking motion).
movement_profile.partnering: Dancers perform in pairs and rejoin partners after the sequence.

signature_moves.name: Manx Balance
signature_moves.description: A distinctive swinging of the foot in a kicking motion.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Flitter Dance: Echoes of the Shore
episode_brief.logline: Discover the ancient Manx tradition of the Flitter Dance, a Good Friday ritual that evolved from beachside fires to the modern stage.
beats: Introduction to the coastal landscape of the Isle of Man.
The history of the Good Friday flitter-gathering custom.
The ritual of the beach fire and the prayer 'Gow shoh as bannee orrin'.
Mona Douglas and the decades-long effort to collect the dance steps.
The 1960 revival by the Manx Folk Dance Society.
Demonstration of the stamping step and the Manx Balance.

claims.text: The Flitter Dance is a traditional dance from the Isle of Man associated with Good Friday.
claims.quote: The Flitter Dance (Flitter Daunsey in Manx) is a traditional dance from the Isle of Man associated with Good Friday.

claims.text: Mona Douglas first mentioned the dance as incomplete in 1937.
claims.quote: A dance was collected in connection to these customs by Mona Douglas, who first mentioned it as ‘partly noted but still incomplete’ in 1937.

claims.text: The dance was collected with the help of informants including Mrs. Teare, Ada Skillicorn, and Mrs. Radcliffe.
claims.quote: By 1957 Douglas had completed the collection of the dance, thanks to material from a Mrs Teare of Ballaugh and in particular from Ada Skillicorn and a Mrs Radcliffe of Maughold

claims.text: The stamping step is thought to be for extinguishing fire embers.
claims.quote: The distinctive stamping step involved is not found in other traditional Manx dances and it was noted by Douglas as being ‘presumably used to stamp out any remaining live embers in the fires.’

claims.text: The dance is performed in a processional form.
claims.quote: No mention is made here of an S-shape to the dance; rather, it is described merely as ‘in processional form.’

claims.text: The dance was revived by the Manx Folk Dance Society in the 1960s.
claims.quote: The dance was brought back into performance in the 1960s by the Manx Folk Dance Society, who also revived the custom of Manx dancing at Easter.
